{#tbl-red-team-program tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

The program covers corrupted requirements and feedback, unauthorized access,
hidden behavior in returned artifacts, triggered workflow components,
supply-chain substitution, visible-check gaming, operational control, and
shared blind spots. Its observations emphasize detection, containment, and
recovery rather than a single pass count.

AgentDojo provides a useful precedent outside hardware. It tests tool-using
agents when untrusted tool returns contain prompt injections
[@DebenedettiEtAl2024AgentDojo]. It does not cover architecture work, but its
attack structure applies to the information-integrity and component-triggered
tests above.

A useful feedback-integrity test places one blocking timing or design-rule
violation inside a long tool report whose candidate identity, conditions, and
other results are valid. The system should preserve and escalate that
violation rather than summarize the report as clean. Record whether it found
the exact violation, prevented acceptance, retained the relevant report
context, and required human review or another tool run to recover.

For every attack, predeclare the attacker access, target surface,
trusted evaluator-owned check, attack budget, and success condition. Also state the
consequence of success, what should detect or interrupt the attack, what counts
as recovery, and which related attacks remain untested. Give the two comparison
arms comparable attack opportunity rather than testing only the system expected
to fail. Pair seeded attacks with clean designs, difficult but benign inputs,
and near-miss triggers. Report trial count and diversity, attack success,
detection, containment, recovery, false alarms, unnecessary stops, clean-task
success, defense overhead, residual failures, uncertainty or an upper bound on
missed failures, untested attacker capabilities, and total recovery cost. Zero
observed failures is not a zero failure rate, and passing one attack class does
not support a general security claim.

An evaluator-awareness test must separate audit visibility from information the
system legitimately needs to solve the task. Use randomized or counterbalanced
matched trials with equivalent usable feedback, while varying whether hidden
review is signaled. Gaming is not any behavioral change. It is improved
visible-check performance accompanied by hidden-requirement violations or
riskier actions under the matched information condition. Clean controls and
near-miss cases are needed to distinguish that pattern from an ordinary
response to different feedback.

For a returned-design test, preserve the artifact and the exact rare input,
state, or sequence that exposed the behavior. For a triggered-component test,
preserve the component version, trigger, surrounding context, proposed or
suppressed action, access used, and downstream artifacts. Replacing or
bypassing the component helps locate the workflow failure. It does not by
itself prove that a returned design is clean, so the artifact checks still run.
For a supply-chain test, preserve expected and observed component identities,
signatures or hashes where available, acquisition path, update event, manifest,
and the dependent caches, checkpoints, artifacts, and claims that must be
invalidated.

Inspectability is a prerequisite for these tests. Evaluator-owned or otherwise
tamper-resistant capture should connect each action to the system version,
candidate state, inputs, tool call, returned result, access decision, human
intervention, cost, and final status. Red-team attempts should try to delete,
rewrite, truncate, or selectively omit that record. When a test fails, the
evaluator must be able to determine what the system used, what it changed, and
which later results may have inherited the failure.

### Exposing Proxy Failure

Before a system spends hours on RTL simulation or physical implementation, it
may use an analytical model or learned predictor to screen candidates. Even a
detailed cycle-level simulator is a lower-fidelity reference for some physical
claims. An optimizer will concentrate on regions where its proxy predicts
improvement, including regions where that proxy's assumptions fail.

The useful measurement is fidelity on a held-out, independently selected
sample near the candidates the system may choose, followed by a
higher-fidelity check on those candidates. Reusing proxy-fitting or
search-selected points for this audit introduces selection bias. Report
uncertainty and decision-relevant errors such as pairwise misranking, retention
of the strongest candidates, and simple regret near the acceptance boundary.
Here, simple regret is the stronger-check objective gap between the selected
candidate and the best candidate audited by that stronger check.

A static held-out sample is insufficient after a search repeatedly queries the
proxy and concentrates on its errors. Preserve an evaluator-selected audit
stream or refreshable holdout, measure stronger-check error on candidates
selected after adaptive search, report how error changes with search budget,
and test whether support or out-of-distribution warnings identify cases the
proxy should decline.

The following documented dispute draws on the original reinforcement-learning
placement result and two later assessments that disagree about the reproduced
setup and conclusion [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement;
@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed].

::: {.callout-war-story title="The placement proxy dispute"}
**The claim.** A reinforcement learning method for chip floorplanning reported
expert-comparable macro placements. It trained against a fast analytical proxy
combining wirelength and estimated congestion rather than waiting for a full
commercial physical-design flow.

**The gap.** An independent assessment of the public Circuit Training
implementation found weak correlation between proxy and post-route outcomes
on its tested cases. Its commercial-flow comparison favored strengthened
simulated annealing, a commercial macro placer, and human placements.
The original authors argued that the assessment
omitted pretraining, used less compute, stopped before convergence, and
evaluated different older-node cases.
Proprietary TPU cases remain a separate reproducibility limit.

**The lesson.** Proxy quality, system identity, and the final implementation
check cannot be separated. When the strongest setup is unavailable, the
disagreement remains limited by that missing comparison.
:::

A placement benchmark such as ChiPBench can make more of the physical-flow
comparison inspectable, but its result remains tied to that flow
[@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench].

### Attacking Constraints and Unrewarded Requirements

An optimizer rewarded for performance and area has an incentive to remove
anything costly that the score does not protect. The simplest attack is not a
better design. It is a weaker task.

The deleted-clock example from @sec-architecture-20-ontology makes the failure
plain. Removing a clock definition can produce a clean timing report because
the intended sequential paths are no longer analyzed. The evaluation must
confirm that required constraints were loaded and unchanged, that the
candidate still implements the declared function, and that the scoring checks
were not modified by the system they judge.

Other attacks remove error correction, memory protection, isolation, or
security mitigations because these features cost power, area, or performance.
The needed check depends on the property. Assertions and model checking can
cover selected single-execution safety properties such as permission
enforcement. Timing and speculative side channels relate multiple executions
and need relational analysis or another check designed for that class. A
generic “formal passed” flag is not enough.

Formal equivalence also has a boundary. It applies when candidate and reference
are intended to have the same observable behavior. Architecture changes that
alter latency, protocols, or permitted behavior need refinement checks,
properties, or another relation that states what may change.

Timing exceptions deserve the same treatment. A false-path or multicycle-path
constraint changes what static timing analysis is asked to check. It is an
assumption, not a timing repair. Credit it only when endpoint-specific timing
intent and protocol or property checks justify the exception. A structural
clock-domain report or documentation alone does not settle it.

Constraint repair also need not improve every count monotonically. Fixing one
setup path may expose a hold path, and routing one net may create a local
spacing violation. The failure is repeated movement among the same states
without progress on the blocking conditions, not every temporary regression.
Eventual burn-down and a recurring count pattern therefore raise different
questions (@fig-whac-a-mole).

```{python}
#| label: fig-whac-a-mole
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **A recurring violation count is a warning, not proof of a repeated design state.** The green illustrative trace burns the blocking timing and design-rule violations down. The red trace settles into a recurring count pattern after an initial improvement. These synthetic counts do not identify the candidate, constraint, violation, or tool state. A real evaluation needs those identities to establish a repeated-state cycle and should not require every useful multi-objective search to be monotonic.
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of blocking timing and design-rule violations over twenty tool iterations. A green illustrative trace declines to zero. A red dashed trace declines at first and then alternates between ten and twenty violations."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

iterations = np.arange(21)
directed = [max(0, int(value)) for value in 50 * np.exp(-0.25 * iterations)]
repeated = [
    int(50 * np.exp(-0.2 * index)) if index < 5 else 15 + 5 * (-1) ** index
    for index in iterations
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.95, top=0.88, bottom=0.18)

ax.plot(
    iterations,
    directed,
    linewidth=2.5,
    color=COLORS["green"],
    label="Directed repair",
)
ax.plot(
    iterations,
    repeated,
    linewidth=2.0,
    linestyle="--",
    color=COLORS["red"],
    label="Recurring violation count",
)

ax.annotate(
    "inspect state identity",
    xy=(10, 20),
    xytext=(11, 31),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["ink"], lw=0.8),
    fontsize=6,
    color=COLORS["ink"],
)

ax.set_title("Constraint repair under repeated feedback", fontsize=7.5, pad=10)
ax.set_xlabel("Tool iteration", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Blocking violations", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_xlim(0, 20)
ax.set_ylim(-2, 55)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=6.5, loc="upper right")
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

Both paths reduce the initial count, but the green path continues toward zero
while the red path settles into a recurring count pattern. That sawtooth is a
warning to inspect the run, not proof that the same design state repeated.
Different candidates can have the same number of blocking violations, and the
same count can hide changes in violation type, endpoint, severity, or
constraint coverage.

Establishing a repeated state requires the candidate or artifact identity, the
loaded constraints, tool and checker versions and settings, seed, violation
identities and severities, relevant checkpoint or tool state, and the action
that led there. A cycle detector can then compare state signatures and action
history rather than treating an equal count as an equal state. The count trace
finds suspicious behavior. The preserved identities determine whether the
workflow actually revisited a state.

### Testing Interruption, Correction, and Recovery

An unattended workflow can turn a small disagreement into a large cost. A
generator may rename a signal to fix lint, trigger equivalence failure, revert
the change, and repeat the original lint failure. Two components can continue
the cycle indefinitely if neither recognizes a repeated state and neither owns
a retry limit.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="A repeated-state loop"}
**The trap.** A proposal component and a checking component repeatedly
alternate between the same lint failure and the same equivalence failure.

**The mechanism.** Each component responds correctly to its immediate input,
but the complete system has no cycle detector, shared retry budget, or stopping
rule for repeated states.

**The lesson.** Evaluation must test whether the complete workflow stops,
releases tool resources, preserves the last trustworthy state, reports why it
stopped, and can resume without restoring the failed action. This is an
illustrative composite failure pattern, not one documented incident.
:::

Operational red-team runs should deliberately trigger tool timeouts and
process kills, queue or scheduler interruption, partial or nominally successful
but incomplete reports, license-feature failures, scratch or database
corruption, stale locks, incompatible incremental checkpoints, missing
analysis modes or corners, and budget exhaustion.
Measure time to detection, actions taken after the fault, ability to revoke
tool access, state preserved for inspection, recovery time, repeated work, and
whether the final evaluation excludes results produced after the failure.

Correction matters as much as interruption. A system that notices a malformed
report but continues from state derived from it is not recovered. The
evaluation should invalidate descendant artifacts and cached results, restore
an evaluator-approved checkpoint, revoke or rotate affected credentials,
release tool and license resources, rerun the affected checks, and trace which
claims were withdrawn or re-established. It should also verify that no poisoned
retrieval entry, script, checkpoint, or tool state remains active. When clean
state cannot be reconstructed, the result remains unresolved.

## A Minimum Complete-System Protocol

A minimum complete-system study can now connect the chapter's pieces.

1. Freeze the two systems, environments, task population, legal actions,
   evaluator-owned checks, and artifact identities.
2. Predeclare primary architecture outcomes, blocking constraints, practical
   margins, resource envelopes, stopping rules, and the treatment of failures.
3. Balance or randomize paired tasks and operators, then keep a held-out
   confirmation set outside system and evaluator tuning.
4. Run both complete workflows while emitting the attempt record in
   @tbl-attempt-cost-record and retaining every assigned task.
5. Promote candidates through declared fidelity stages and audit cheap screens
   against checks capable of observing the property at risk.
6. Estimate paired task-level outcome and cost differences with uncertainty,
   including failures, censored runs, and heterogeneous task effects.
7. Run the declared sensitivity, component, benchmark-integrity, and red-team
   tests under comparable opportunity.
8. Report the claim as supported, unsupported, or unresolved, together with
   the tasks, conditions, costs, checks, and transfer limits that produced that
   status.

This protocol is connective tissue, not a universal experiment template. An
RTL optimization study may progress from lint and simulation through synthesis
and place and route, while a system-architecture study uses different checks.
Both still preserve task identity, comparable budgets, attempt-level cost,
fidelity promotion, and a final claim bounded by what actually ran.

## Reporting What the Evaluation Supports

A complete-system evaluation combines results across tasks with the matched
comparison, costs, component tests, varied conditions, and attacks needed to
judge the AI-assisted system. It should contain the fields in
@tbl-complete-system-assessment.

| **Evaluation field** | **Required content** |
| --- | --- |
| Complete-system identity | Versioned AI-assisted workflow, represented information, methods, legal action space, tools, checks, people, budgets, and stopping rules |
| Matched alternative | Strongest practical conventional or human-directed workflow and any remaining mismatch |
| Benchmark identity and health | Task and benchmark versions, remaining contamination risk, refresh or retirement status, fidelity depth, and aggregation policy |
| Architecture outcomes | Per-task supported results, failures, verification depth, maintainability, integration and change burden, comparators, uncertainty, and nonclaims; manufacturability, test, packaging, and bring-up evidence when the decision reaches silicon |
| Coordination and decision quality | Role, state, information-use, tool, interpretation, and control failures; retrieval quality; useful observations; supported decisions; false accepts and rejects; escalation, stopping, recovery, and human overrides |
| Incremental AI contribution | Difference in result quality, total cost, or both, with the comparison that supports it |
| Total cost | Observed human setup, operation, review and decision work, model and general compute, data and samples, engineering tools by type and stage, verification, integration, recovery, and elapsed time; one-time amortized work and projected future change burden reported separately |
| Reliability and robustness | Repeated-run success and failure distributions, calibration, worst cases, constraint violations, recovery and override behavior, apparatus sensitivity, and behavior under declared perturbations |
| Transfer limits | Conditions where the result repeated, failed, or was not tested |
| Component dependencies | Ablations, selected interactions, human intervention, and unresolved attribution |
| Red-team results | Threat-model coverage; attacks and benign controls attempted against returned artifacts, workflow components, authority boundaries, and protected records; invalid acceptances, unauthorized access, false alarms, detection, interruption, correction, containment, recovery, defense cost, and residual uncertainty |
| Program status | Supported, unsupported, or unresolved claim within named tasks, conditions, budgets, and checks |

: **The final output states what the complete-system evaluation supports.** It
gives architects the result needed for a responsibility and commitment
decision without making that decision itself.
{#tbl-complete-system-assessment tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The assessment keeps system identity, benchmark health, architecture outcome,
decision behavior, incremental contribution, cost, reliability, dependencies,
attacks, and transfer limits separately inspectable. Program status comes last
because it summarizes the tested evidence without authorizing architecture
commitment.

The three status terms need explicit rules.

**Supported.** Across the predeclared task and condition coverage, repeated
matched comparisons show either an architecture improvement that clears the
minimum worthwhile effect within the acceptable total-cost envelope, or a cost
reduction that clears its declared margin while architecture quality remains
within the noninferiority margin. The paired effect and its uncertainty must
clear the relevant decision boundary. The component dependencies, failures,
attacks, and uncertainty must also be understood well enough to support the
claim.

**Unsupported.** Matched comparisons with the declared task coverage and
resolving power show neither a worthwhile architecture improvement within the
acceptable cost envelope nor the required cost reduction at noninferior
quality, or directly contradict the narrower claim being tested. A successful
artifact can coexist with an unsupported AI-contribution claim.

**Unresolved.** The credible alternative was not run, uncertainty obscures the
difference, important costs were omitted, the task set is too narrow, a
comparison lacks the resolving power to distinguish the declared margins, a
paired interval overlaps the decision boundary, a disqualifying stage was not
reached, or red-team failures leave the result unreadable. Unresolved is not a
polite form of supported.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The current Lighthouse evaluation"}
The current manuscript does not contain the matched, repeated,
implementation-facing comparison required to close the Lighthouse program
test. @sec-running-the-loop supplies one limited simulator study.
@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack shows why its local no-change result
cannot justify freezing the array and interface and defines the target tests.
No complete AI-assisted and credible alternative systems have yet run that
target evaluation across the required conditions.

The implementation-facing architecture outcome is therefore unresolved. The
incremental contribution of AI is unresolved. The moonshot program status is
also unresolved. This evaluation is useful because it identifies the exact
comparison, costs, conditions, and attacks needed to change that status.

The current evaluation contains the declared target, the simulator result,
its transfer limits, the required implementation-facing tests, and these
unresolved statuses. It does not contain versioned complete-system comparison
arms, matched total costs, repeated-run reliability, implementation-facing
attack results, or a closed contribution estimate.
:::

This status does not grant or withhold permission. A supported system-level
claim can still leave residual risks an organization refuses to accept. An
unsupported AI-contribution claim can still accompany a sound architecture
produced by conventional work. The architect receives this evaluation and its
named missing conditions. @sec-what-architect-owns takes up the separate
question of authority, residual risk, and architecture commitment.

## Open Research Questions

Evaluating an AI-assisted design system requires comparable architecture
outcomes, complete cost accounting, reliable behavior, and tests that expose
how the system fails.

**Credible program comparison.** The comparison must remain meaningful across
tasks and organizations without hiding the resources or decisions that differ.

**How should total architecture-workflow cost be compared across
organizations?** Labor, tool access, queueing, data, and schedule consequences
do not share one natural unit, and a single dollar value can conceal the
resource that actually limits the work.

**How can an architecture benchmark remain representative as models, tools,
workloads, and design practices change without losing comparability across
versions?** Refresh is necessary to limit contamination and decay, but frequent
change can make longitudinal results uninterpretable.

**Attribution and reliability.** A complete workflow contains interacting
learned components, conventional tools, and human intervention whose effects
may not separate cleanly.

**How can improvement be attributed among interacting system components
without an infeasible number of ablations?** One-at-a-time replacement misses
interactions, while exhaustive combinations can cost more than the architecture
work being evaluated.

**Which variations are most predictive of failure when an AI-assisted system
enters a new design program?** Repeated runs on one task measure only a narrow
form of reliability, while broad variation across designs, tools, and operating
conditions is expensive.

**Adversarial evaluation.** Red teaming should reveal consequential failures
that ordinary tasks and visible checks do not expose.

**Which red-team tests best predict failures in real architecture workflows?**
Reproducible synthetic attacks are useful, but their value depends on whether
they expose unsafe design changes, corrupted checks, bad tool actions, or
recovery failures that also arise in practice.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Evaluate the result, workflow, cost, and limits"}
Judge an AI-assisted design workflow by the architecture it produces, the
quality of its decisions, its total cost, and the conditions under which its
advantage survives. Compare complete workflows and attack their assumptions
before stating what they improve.
:::

Evaluation separates the candidate architecture, configured technical design
system, and complete workflow. The architecture result shows what the workflow
achieved. Coordination and decision measures show whether it selected suitable
methods and tools, preserved state, interpreted results correctly, and
escalated when needed. Total cost shows whether a local speedup survived model
use, data preparation, tools, verification, integration, review, recovery, and
future change work.

A credible comparison holds the architecture question and evaluator-owned
checks fixed while comparing the strongest practical complete workflows.
Repeated runs and varied conditions reveal whether the advantage survives
changes in prompts, seeds, workloads, designs, tools, and operating conditions.
Component replacements locate dependencies without pretending that
interacting parts make independent, additive contributions. Healthy benchmarks
keep these comparisons readable through clear identity, representative tasks,
contamination controls, versioning, refresh, retirement, and reproducible
reporting.

Red teaming completes the evaluation. A system must face altered requirements,
weakened checks, misleading feedback, hidden behavior inserted into returned
designs, triggered misbehavior in workflow components, repeated-state loops,
and failures of interruption and recovery. The result is not a universal trust
score. It is a qualified account of where the system works, what it costs, what
it depends on, and how it fails.

For the current Lighthouse program, that account remains unresolved. The
matched complete-system comparison has not been run across the target
conditions and implementation checks. The resulting evaluation record can
inform an architecture commitment, but it does not authorize one. The
remaining question is what architects contribute, decide, and remain
responsible for when the technical system can do substantial work.
